summary: Specifies using the SM2 digital signature algorithm and the SM3 hash algorithm for DNSSEC. It is an Independent Submission to the RFC series and does not have IETF community consensus.

eli5.summary: DNS records can be sealed to show they are genuine. This describes sealing them with a signature method from China, though IETF people did not all agree on it.

questions: how to use sm2 in dnssec
subtitle: Digital signature method using SM2 elliptic curves and SM3 hashing

tldr.problem: DNSSEC authenticates DNS records using cryptographic signatures. Different regions use different cryptographic standards, and China has national standards for elliptic curve signatures.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds support for SM2 (an elliptic curve signature algorithm) and SM3 (a hash function) to DNSSEC, allowing DNS zones to sign their records with these Chinese standard algorithms.
tldr.outcome: DNSSEC validators can now verify signatures made with SM2, though this is an independent submission and does not have broad IETF consensus.

today: RFC 9563 is an Informational document that is not an IETF standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines an optional algorithm for DNSSEC that deployers may choose to implement, primarily for use in regions where SM2 and SM3 are preferred standards.

sections.title: Introduction to SM2 for DNSSEC
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records to prove they are authentic. Every DNSSEC deployment uses cryptographic keys and signatures. The RFC specifies that SM2 (an elliptic curve algorithm) and SM3 (a hash function) can be used as signing algorithms for DNSSEC records.

SM2 and SM3 are national standards for China, defined in the GM/T standards and also published as ISO/IEC standards (ISO/IEC 14888-3 for SM2 and ISO/IEC 10118-3 for SM3). Both the public key and the hash output are 256 bits, matching the same security level. This is an independent submission to the RFC series; it has not received consensus from the broader IETF community.
sections.eli5: DNSSEC adds a signature to DNS records to prove they are real. This RFC adds a way to make those signatures using SM2, which is a signature method from China.

sections.title: SM2 and SM3 Algorithms
sections.content:
SM2 is a digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curves over a 256-bit prime field. The curve parameters are specified in the document and match the ISO/IEC 14888-3 standard. SM2 signatures consist of two integers, called r and s, each 32 octets (256 bits) when encoded.

SM3 is a cryptographic hash function that produces a 256-bit digest. It follows the same pattern as other hash-based DS (Delegation Signer) records in DNSSEC, with digest type code 6, similar to how SHA-256 uses digest type 2.
sections.eli5: SM2 is a math trick for creating signatures. SM3 is a way to turn a long message into a short fingerprint. Both are from Chinese standards instead of American or European ones.

sections.title: DNSSEC Record Formats
sections.content:
In DNSSEC, SM2 public keys (called P) are stored as 64 octets representing the uncompressed form of the elliptic curve point: the x-coordinate and y-coordinate concatenated. This matches the SM2 specification in GM/T 0003.1.

SM2 signatures in RRSIG records are the concatenation of r | s, where each value is formatted as 32 octets. The algorithm number assigned to SM2 in DNSSEC is 17, registered with IANA as mnemonic SM2SM3.

For negative proof of existence, zones using SM2 must also support NSEC or NSEC3 records. If using NSEC3 denial of existence with SM2, the hash iterations MUST be 0 and the salt MUST be empty, as recommended in RFC 9276.
sections.eli5: When storing an SM2 key in DNS, you write the key as 64 bytes. When signing, you write the signature as two 64-byte numbers in a row. DNS can use this to say a domain name does not exist by hashing the name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security strength of SM2 depends on the key size. A 256-bit key provides 256-bit security strength. The security of any elliptic curve algorithm also depends on the specific curve chosen; in this case, the SM2 curve is specified in the standards documents.

If a weakness is discovered in SM2 or SM3, the remedy is crypto-agility: the ability to switch to a different algorithm. For DNSSEC, this means generating new DS, DNSKEY, RRSIG, and NSEC3 records with a different algorithm and carefully managing the key rollover to account for DNS caching (as detailed in RFC 7583).

The broader caution from the document is that this is not an IETF standard and does not have community consensus. Neither the IETF nor the IRTF has formally analyzed SM2 for suitability, and the algorithm may contain either intended or unintended weaknesses.
sections.eli5: SM2 signatures are only strong if the secret key stays secret. If someone finds a way to break SM2 in the future, you would switch to a different signature method. The IETF did not fully review this to say it is safe.

sections.title: Compatibility and Deployment
sections.content:
Many DNSSEC validators will not support SM2 signatures and SM3 digests when this RFC is published. RFC 6840 specifies how DNSSEC resolvers should handle signatures with unsupported algorithms: they should treat them as correctly signed even if the resolver cannot itself verify them.

Implementations are free to support SM2; the RFC permits (MAY, not MUST) both DNSSEC signers and verifiers to implement the SM2 and SM3 algorithms. This allows gradual, optional adoption in zones that need it while other zones can continue using more widely supported algorithms like RSASHA256 or ECDSAP256SHA256.
sections.eli5: Not all DNS systems will know how to check SM2 signatures right away. DNS allows this by letting some people use SM2 while others use more common signature methods.
